특히 채권시장이 주목하는 것은 경유 가격이다. 2일 미국의 전국 평균 경유 소매가격은 갤런당 5.68달러를 넘어섰다. 1년 전보다 약 2달러 비싸다. 페르시아만에서 전투가 벌어지고 호르무즈 해협 통행이 막혔던 올봄 최고치와 1센트도 차이가 나지 않는다. 러시아의 우크라이나 침공으로 에너지 가격이 폭등했던 2022년 기록과도 13센트 차이에 불과하다.
앞으로 가격이 더 오를 가능성도 있다. 10월 인도분 디젤 선물가격은 최근 일주일 동안 약 13% 상승했다.
경유값 상승은 휘발유보다 경제 전반에 미치는 파장이 크다. 경유는 트럭과 열차, 건설장비, 농기계 등에 광범위하게 사용된다. 가격이 오르면 운송비와 생산비가 함께 뛰면서 식료품과 공산품 등 각종 상품 가격으로 번질 수 있다.
마이크 구세이 프린시펄자산운용 최고투자책임자(CIO)는 “전 세계 채권 수익률의 급격한 상승은 투자자들이 인플레이션을 재평가하고 있음을 반영한다”고 말했다.
채권 투자자에게 인플레이션은 가장 큰 적이다. 채권은 미리 정해진 이자를 지급하기 때문에 물가가 오를수록 투자자가 얻는 실질 수익은 줄어든다. 인플레이션이 오래갈 것으로 예상할수록 투자자들은 국채를 사는 대가로 더 높은 금리를 요구한다.
② 40조달러 빚…쏟아지는 국채 누가 사나
두 번째 압력은 미국 정부의 재정이다.
미국의 국가부채는 지난달 사상 처음 40조달러를 돌파했다. 국내총생산(GDP) 대비 공공부채 비율도 제2차 세계대전 이후 볼 수 없었던 수준을 향해 빠르게 올라가고 있다.
빚이 늘어날수록 미국 정부는 더 많은 국채를 발행해야 한다. 시장에 국채 공급이 늘어나는 속도만큼 수요가 따라오지 못하면 국채 가격은 떨어지고 수익률은 상승한다.
높은 금리는 다시 미국의 재정 부담을 키운다. 과거 연 1~2%대의 낮은 금리로 발행했던 국채가 만기를 맞으면 현재의 높은 금리로 차환해야 하기 때문이다. 저금리 빚이 하나씩 고금리 빚으로 바뀌는 셈이다.
미국 정부가 한 해 지급하는 이자비용은 이미 국방비를 넘어섰다. 제2차 세계대전 이후 보기 드문 상황이다.
재정 우려는 미국만의 문제도 아니다. 영국에서는 국채금리 급등이 정부에 부채 감축 압력으로 작용하고 있다. 일본에서는 감세 논쟁과 재정 악화 우려가 맞물리면서 10년 만기 국채금리가 약 30년 만의 최고 수준까지 올라섰다.
각국 정부가 빚을 내기 위해 동시에 대규모 국채를 쏟아내면서 글로벌 채권 투자자의 돈을 놓고 경쟁하는 상황이 벌어지고 있는 것이다.
③ “10년·30년 빌리려면 더 줘”…기간 프리미엄 상승
세 번째는 ‘기간 프리미엄’이다.
기간 프리미엄은 투자자가 장기간 채권에 돈을 묶어두면서 감수해야 하는 위험의 대가로 요구하는 추가 금리다.
쉽게 말하면 투자자가 미국 정부에 “앞으로 10년이나 30년 동안 돈을 빌려주려면 이자를 더 달라”고 요구하는 것이다.
앞으로 물가가 얼마나 오를지, 정부가 국채를 얼마나 더 발행할지, 재정적자가 얼마나 커질지 알기 어려울수록 이 프리미엄은 높아진다.
최근 미국의 기간 프리미엄은 상승세를 보이고 있다. 특히 이란 전쟁 이후 변화가 두드러졌다. 전쟁이 장기화해 에너지 가격과 인플레이션이 더 오를 가능성을 투자자들이 장기 국채 가격에 반영하고 있다는 의미다.
유럽과 일본에서도 장기채 기간 프리미엄이 높아지고 있다. 미국만의 현상이 아니라 글로벌 채권시장에서 ‘오래 돈을 빌려주는 위험’의 가격 자체가 비싸지고 있는 셈이다.
인공지능(AI) 투자 열풍도 국채 수급에 부담을 더하고 있다. 빅테크와 AI 관련 기업들이 데이터센터와 전력 인프라 구축 자금을 마련하기 위해 회사채를 대거 발행하면서 투자자들의 자금을 놓고 국채와 경쟁하고 있어서다.
전 세계 AI 관련 채권 발행 규모는 약 5000억달러에 달한다. 다만 로빈 위글스워스 파이낸셜타임스(FT) 알파빌 편집장은 AI 채권 발행이 국채금리를 일부 밀어올릴 수는 있지만 재정과 인플레이션에 비하면 영향은 제한적이라고 분석했다.
④ ‘워시의 Fed’ 어디로…불확실성에도 금리 붙었다
마지막 압력은 Fed다.
워시 의장은 지난달 말 잭슨홀 연설에서 인플레이션 억제에 대한 의지를 드러내면서 Fed가 물가에 충분히 강경하지 않을 수 있다는 시장의 우려를 일부 누그러뜨렸다.
하지만 전임자들과 달리 앞으로의 구체적인 금리 경로에 대해서는 뚜렷한 신호를 주지 않았다.
Fed가 어느 정도의 금리를 적정 수준으로 판단하는지, 물가가 다시 오르면 얼마나 적극적으로 대응할지 시장이 예측하기 어려워진 것이다. 이런 불확실성 자체가 장기 국채금리에 새로운 위험 프리미엄으로 붙고 있다는 분석이다.
데이비드 켈리 JP모건자산운용 수석 글로벌 전략가는 “몇 달 전과 확연히 달라진 점을 하나 꼽으라면 케빈 워시가 Fed 의장으로 취임한 이후 Fed의 행보”라며 “비록 작은 규모일지라도 Fed의 위험 프리미엄이 시장에 더해졌다고 본다”고 말했다.
채권을 짓누르는 압력이 한꺼번에 커지자 도널드 트럼프 행정부도 시장에 직접 손을 대기 시작했다.
스콧 베센트 미 재무장관은 장기 국채 매입 확대 카드를 꺼냈다. 재무부가 거래가 상대적으로 뜸한 기존 국채를 사들이면서 시장 유동성을 높이고 국채금리 상승을 억제하려는 시도다.
하지만 약발은 오래가지 않았다. 발표 직후 국채금리가 잠시 떨어졌지만 이내 다시 상승했다.
미 국채시장은 약 32조달러 규모로 하루 거래액만 1조달러를 넘는다. 재무부가 수십억달러 규모의 국채를 추가로 사들이는 것만으로 전체 시장의 방향을 돌리기에는 역부족이라는 평가다.
위글스워스 편집장은 재무부의 국채 매입을 “물총으로 산불을 끄는 것과 같다”고 평가했다.
켈리 수석 전략가도 베센트 장관의 대응을 신용카드에 빗댔다. 그는 정부가 세금을 올리고 지출을 줄여 재정적자를 축소하는 것이 아니라 국채 매입 여력만 늘리는 것은 “이미 20개나 되는 신용카드 가운데 한도까지 다 쓰지 않은 카드 하나를 더 찾아낸 것”과 같다고 지적했다.
문제는 네 가지 압력이 따로 움직이는 것이 아니라 서로를 밀어올린다는 점이다.
전쟁이 길어지면 에너지 가격과 물가가 오르고, 인플레이션이 높아지면 Fed가 금리를 낮출 여지는 줄어든다. 높은 금리는 40조달러를 넘어선 미국 정부의 이자 부담을 키우고, 재정에 대한 우려가 커지면 투자자들은 장기 국채를 보유하는 대가로 더 높은 기간 프리미엄을 요구한다.
headline: ①전쟁 ②40조달러 빚 ③기간 프리미엄 ④워시 … 채권 짓누르는  4대 압력 [ 디브리핑 ]
Lives on hold : Young Iranians watch their futures slip away

body:
Війни в Україні та Ірані дедалі тісніше переплітаються і створюють ризик ширшої ескалації, вважає старший науковий співробітник "Фонду Карнегі за міжнародний мир" Крістофер Чіввіс. У своїй колонці для The Guardian він звертає увагу на низку подій, які свідчать про поступове зближення двох конфліктів та зростання небезпеки їхнього взаємного впливу.
Автор починає з ситуації навколо України. За його словами, Росія поки не спричинила масових жертв серед європейців за межами України, однак наближається до цього сценарію. Чіввіс згадує події на початку серпня біля аеропорту Лейпциг/Галле в Німеччині, де неподалік злітно-посадкової смуги виявили два заміновані безпілотники. Автор нагадує, що ще у 2024 році на цьому ж аеропорті запалювальні пристрої, заховані в посилках, спричинили займання вантажу компанії DHL.
На думку Чіввіса, саме інцидент з дронами в Лейпцигу міг стати однією з причин поїздки директора ЦРУ Джона Реткліффа до Москви наприкінці серпня. Як писали ЗМІ, під час зустрічей він попереджав російську сторону про неприпустимість атак на територію НАТО, закликав скоротити підтримку Ірану та наголошував на необхідності домовленостей щодо завершення війни проти України.
"Проте відмова адміністрації Трампа припинити війну з Іраном працює врозріз із її зусиллями завершити війну в Україні. Вони прямують у шторм, а не виходять із нього", - пише аналітик.
Автор також звертає увагу на виснаження американських запасів ракет-перехоплювачів через війну з Іраном. На його думку, повідомлення про суттєве скорочення запасів і поставок засобів протиповітряної оборони в Україну могли переконати Володимира Путіна, що США знову відволікаються на Близький Схід. Це, своєю чергою, може створити для Кремля сприятливе вікно можливостей для посилення ударів по Україні.
Водночас Україна вже безпосередньо залучена до протистояння з Іраном. Як зазначає Чіввіс, Київ направив до країн Перської затоки 228 спеціалістів і значні партії безпілотників для допомоги у відбитті іранських дронових атак. Крім того, наприкінці липня Україна завдала удару по іранському вантажному судну в Каспійському морі. Росія зі свого боку передавала Ірану розвідувальну інформацію, яка могла підвищити ефективність його ударів, а сама Москва давно використовує розроблені в Ірані безпілотники у війні проти України.
"Обидва конфлікти одночасно погіршуються і нікуди не рухаються", - констатує аналітик. Саме це, на думку автора, створює найбільшу небезпеку: сторони можуть дедалі більше покладатися на військову силу, намагаючись виправдати вже понесені втрати та витрати.
Чіввіс також згадує посилення координації між Росією, Китаєм та Іраном. Володимир Путін і Сі Цзіньпін зустрілися напередодні саміту Шанхайської організації співробітництва, де також мають бути присутні представники Ірану. За оцінкою автора, Пекін не обов’язково зацікавлений у продовженні обох війн, але водночас не хоче поразки Росії чи Ірану і має можливості допомагати їм пом’якшувати наслідки конфліктів.
Чіввіс вважає, що одного дипломатичного попередження Москві недостатньо. Він закликає Вашингтон шукати реальні стимули для припинення обох війн, зокрема домовлятися з Іраном про припинення вогню, санкційне послаблення та розмороження активів. Щодо України автор пропонує серйозніше обговорити питання нейтралітету та доцільність подальшої боротьби за території Донбасу, які залишаються під контролем Києва.
У фіналі публікації експерт посилається на історика Одда Арне Вестада, який порівнює сучасну ситуацію зі світом напередодні Першої світової війни.
"Ключовий урок світу перед 1914 роком полягає в тому, що регіональні конфлікти, які довго залишаються невирішеними, можуть стати пороховими діжками, що спричинять глобальне загоряння", - йдеться в попередженні.
На думку Чіввіса, саме переплетення війни Росії проти України з конфліктом навколо Ірану робить нинішню ситуацію особливо небезпечною. Він закликає світових лідерів серйозніше поставитися до цих ризиків, поки регіональні війни не переросли у значно масштабнішу кризу.
Війна в Україні: перспективи миру
Як писав УНІАН, на думку оглядачів, заяви Володимира Путіна на саміті ШОС у Бішкеку свідчать про його жорстку позицію щодо війни в Україні та відсутність готовності до компромісів. Диктатор порівняв конфронтацію із Заходом із боротьбою за виживання у "харчовому ланцюгу".
Тим часом міністр закордонних справ України Андрій Сибіга заявив, що очікує нової динаміки у мирних зусиллях щодо припинення російської агресії. Він наголосив, що дипломатія має відігравати активнішу роль і що досягти результату неможливо без участі США, з якими Україна підтримує постійний діалог.
headline: Війна в Україні та конфлікт з Іраном загрожують світу неконтрольованою ескалацією

body:
Войны в Украине и Иране все теснее переплетаются и создают риск более широкой эскалации, считает старший научный сотрудник "Фонда Карнеги за международный мир" Кристофер Чиввис. В своей колонке для The Guardian он обращает внимание на ряд событий, свидетельствующих о постепенном сближении двух конфликтов и росте опасности их взаимного влияния.
Автор начинает с ситуации вокруг Украины. По его словам, Россия пока не причинила массовых жертв среди европейцев за пределами Украины, однако приближается к этому сценарию. Чиввис упоминает события в начале августа возле аэропорта Лейпциг/Галле в Германии, где недалеко от взлетно-посадочной полосы обнаружили два заминированных беспилотника. Автор напоминает, что ещё в 2024 году в этом же аэропорту зажигательные устройства, спрятанные в посылках, привели к возгоранию груза компании DHL.
По мнению Чиввиса, именно инцидент с дронами в Лейпциге мог стать одной из причин поездки директора ЦРУ Джона Ретклиффа в Москву в конце августа. Как писали СМИ, во время встреч он предупреждал российскую сторону о недопустимости атак на территорию НАТО, призывал сократить поддержку Ирана и подчеркивал необходимость договоренностей о завершении войны против Украины.
"Однако отказ администрации Трампа прекратить войну с Ираном идет вразрез с её усилиями по прекращению войны в Украине. Они направляются в шторм, а не выходят из него", – пишет аналитик.
Автор также обращает внимание на истощение американских запасов ракет-перехватчиков из-за войны с Ираном. По его мнению, сообщения о существенном сокращении запасов и поставок средств противовоздушной обороны в Украину могли убедить Владимира Путина в том, что США вновь отвлекаются на Ближний Восток. Это, в свою очередь, может создать для Кремля благоприятное окно возможностей для усиления ударов по Украине.
В то же время Украина уже непосредственно вовлечена в противостояние с Ираном. Как отмечает Чиввис, Киев направил в страны Персидского залива 228 специалистов и значительные партии беспилотников для помощи в отражении иранских дроновых атак. Кроме того, в конце июля Украина нанесла удар по иранскому грузовому судну в Каспийском море. Россия, со своей стороны, передавала Ирану разведывательную информацию, которая могла повысить эффективность его ударов, а сама Москва давно использует разработанные в Иране беспилотники в войне против Украины.
"Оба конфликта одновременно обостряются и никуда не движутся", – констатирует аналитик. Именно это, по мнению автора, создает наибольшую опасность: стороны могут все больше полагаться на военную силу, пытаясь оправдать уже понесенные потери и затраты.
Чиввис также упоминает усиление координации между Россией, Китаем и Ираном. Владимир Путин и Си Цзиньпин встретились накануне саммита Шанхайской организации сотрудничества, где также должны присутствовать представители Ирана. По оценке автора, Пекин не обязательно заинтересован в продолжении обеих войн, но в то же время не хочет поражения России или Ирана и имеет возможности помогать им смягчать последствия конфликтов.
Чиввис считает, что одного дипломатического предупреждения Москве недостаточно. Он призывает Вашингтон искать реальные стимулы для прекращения обеих войн, в частности договариваться с Ираном о прекращении огня, ослаблении санкций и размораживании активов. Что касается Украины, автор предлагает более серьёзно обсудить вопрос о нейтралитете и целесообразности дальнейшей борьбы за территории Донбасса, которые остаются под контролем Киева.
В заключительной части публикации эксперт ссылается на историка Одда Арне Вестада, который сравнивает современную ситуацию с миром накануне Первой мировой войны.
"Ключевой урок мира перед 1914 годом заключается в том, что региональные конфликты, которые долго остаются нерешенными, могут стать пороховыми бочками, которые вызовут глобальный пожар", – говорится в предупреждении.
По мнению Чиввиса, именно переплетение войны России против Украины с конфликтом вокруг Ирана делает нынешнюю ситуацию особенно опасной. Он призывает мировых лидеров более серьёзно отнестись к этим рискам, пока региональные войны не переросли в гораздо более масштабный кризис.

The Saudi -led coalition fighting the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels said Thursday it has thwarted a missile attack on the holy city of Medina as well as another attack in the eastern part of the kingdom.
Meanwhile, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed one man, hospital officials said.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Thursday. Read our full coverage here.
Houthis deny responsibility for new attack on holy city
The Saudi-led coalition confirmed in a statement that it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile over the province of Medina, but notably did not assign blame for the attack.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree denied carrying out the attack. The rebel group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Medina is where the Prophet Muhammad established the Muslim community, while Mecca is where the prophet was born and received his revelations. It's viewed as the holiest city in Islam.
The international airport in the capital, Riyadh, has suspended service because of Houthi attacks. Dozens of flights also were canceled or delayed at Jeddah airport, according to Flightradar24, a flight tracking platform.
Earlier Thursday, Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over Eastern province, a major oil-producing region.
The latest conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transport of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to retake them.
Deploying Turkish forces to help Saudis needs parliament approval
Turkey’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that a mutual defense pact between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, as well as any deployment of Turkish forces under the agreement, requires parliamentary approval.
In a statement, the ministry also indicated that no final decision had been made on the type of assistance Turkey might provide to Saudi Arabia.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, and Turkish officials say it is expected to be ratified by parliament in the coming days. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and other officials have ruled out the deployment of combat troops, stressing that the pact is purely defensive.
Israel carries out deadly strike in Gaza
An Israeli strike north of Gaza City killed one man on Thursday morning, according to officials at Shifa Hospital.
Israel’s military said it struck a “terrorist” in the area, without elaborating.
The strike came over a year after a ceasefire deal was reached between Israel and the Hamas militant group, a period during which Israel continued to launch deadly strikes on the enclave.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire was reached in October last year, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Syria sentences 5 over last year’s coastal violence
A Syrian court on Thursday sentenced two people to death and three others to prison terms over their roles in last year's sectarian violence in the country’s coastal region.
In March 2025, loyalists of ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad attacked members of the new government’s security forces in areas where a large segment of the country’s Alawite religious minority live. The government’s counterinsurgency spiraled into widespread violence in which hundreds of civilians — most of them Alawites — were killed.
Two members of the pro-Assad groups were sentenced to death and a third to 12 years in prison. Two members of the security forces received prison terms.
EU-GCC meeting has been postponed
The European Union announced in a statement that the joint meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council members set for Oct. 24 in the Saudi capital has been pushed back.
No new date has been set for the gathering that would bring together leaders from the 27 EU economies and the Gulf states of Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates
The EU did not explain why the meeting was being delayed, but the security situation in Riyadh remains uncertain following back-and-forth strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

The EU did not explain why the meeting was being delayed, but the security situation in Riyadh remains uncertain following back-and-forth strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition. 
( Source : AP )

How the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point
DUBAI, Oct 15 - The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.
By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions, they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran's economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources.
The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia's prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb in the Red Sea.
Iran, under mounting economic and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington's strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage.
“The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability.
The Houthis have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends.
But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognised government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen.
A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks would continue unless Saudi restrictions were lifted.
The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that could undermine his transformation agenda, but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030.
The Saudi government media office and Iran's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran's behest, saying its demands were centred on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants' salaries from Yemen's own resources.
"Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else," he said.
FLAGSHIP CONFERENCES DISRUPTED
Saudi Arabia has faced a widening wave of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a strike on Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors.
The attacks have disrupted Riyadh's flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives to withdraw, and forced organisers to offer remote participation at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum.
The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire.
However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. "They reached a point of NO negotiations," he said. "They have no other choice except military action."
The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. "What the Houthis are asking now is a victor's peace," he said.
The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington's reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome.
SAUDIS HAVE MORE TO LOSE
At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS asked Trump for help to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while appearing to defer any response until after the US midterm elections.
The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defences, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favour them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group's advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake.
"Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure," he said. "They have so much less to lose than the Saudis."
Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis' campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula.
At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unravelling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran.
"We're heading towards the worst outcome imaginable," al-Muslimi said. "A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies."
He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. "The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone," he said. "They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war." REUTERS

body:
Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Houthis attempt to raise the cost of the Yemen war for Saudi Arabia as attacks, fighting intensify.
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.
headline: Fighting in Yemen intensifies : What the latest on the battlefield ? | Houthis News

Saudi Arabia says it thwarted a missile strike on Medina, and other Middle East developments
The Saudi -led coalition fighting the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said it thwarted a missile attack on the holy city of Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed an attack in the port city of Aden at a site used by the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government, where an official said at least two people were killed. And a former chief of Israel’s domestic security service has filed a defamation suit against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Thursday. Read our full coverage here.
The Saudi-led coalition said in a statement that it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile over the province of Medina, but notably did not assign blame for the attack.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree denied carrying out the attack. The rebel group previously pledged not to attack airports in the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
The latest conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for oil shipments. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to retake those areas.
Houthi-launched missiles and drones struck Thursday near the palace used by Yemen’s recognized government in the port city of Aden, with an official saying at least two people had been killed.
Another six people were wounded, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility.
Many of Yemen’s government leaders live in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official said.
- Ahmed Al Haj in Aden, Yemen
The 15 members of the U.N.’s most powerful body issue few unanimous statements on global conflicts and other issues. But the council condemned “in the strongest terms” the ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, saying the strikes on civilian airports and other facilities have been “reckless.”
The statement said the council expressed their solidarity with Saudi Arabia and "affirmed the inherent right of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of self-defence in accordance with international law.”
A former chief of Israel’s domestic security service filed a defamation suit against Netanyahu, saying the prime minister had falsely accused him of withholding warnings about Hamas threats before the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.
Ronen Bar, former head of the agency commonly known as Shin Bet, demanded 3 million shekels ($965,000) in the suit filed Wednesday.
Netanyahu, in a post last month on X, accused Bar of “failures and crimes” in the hours before the attack, when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people and took 251 hostages, setting off a massive Israeli bombardment and invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Netanyahu said Bar knew of the Hamas threat but didn’t inform him, the military or civilian security units.
Bar called the accusations “blood libel,” detailing the steps he took in the hours before the attack to update Netanyahu’s top military advisers and the army, and describes a series of warnings and recommendations his agency delivered in the months before the attack which he says were “consistently disregarded” by the prime minister.
After a string of resignations by top security officials -- including Bar -- Netanyahu remains the only senior figure from Oct. 7 still in office.
An Israeli strike north of Gaza City killed one man, according to officials at Shifa Hospital.
Israel’s military said it struck a “terrorist” in the area, without elaborating.
The strike came over a year after a ceasefire deal was reached between Israel and the Hamas militant group, a period during which Israel continued to launch deadly strikes on the enclave.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire was reached in October last year, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
A Syrian court sentenced two people to death and three others to prison terms over their roles in last year's sectarian violence in the country’s coastal region.
In March 2025, loyalists of ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad attacked members of the new government’s security forces in areas where a large segment of the country’s Alawite religious minority lives. The government’s counterinsurgency spiraled into widespread violence in which hundreds of civilians — most of them Alawites — were killed.
Two members of the pro-Assad groups were sentenced to death and a third to 12 years in prison. Two members of the security forces received prison terms.

International News Briefs for Thursday, October 15, 2026
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Thursday, October 15, 2026.
WFP Warns Growing Conflict in Yemen Has Cut Off Aid Deliveries to 800,000 People
Oct 15, 2026
The United Nations warns some 800,000 people have been cut off from lifesaving assistance due to heavy fighting between Houthi militias and Saudi-backed forces. The World Food Programme says shifting frontlines, blocked roads and growing insecurity have severely hampered access to the city of Taiz, which is encircled by Houthi militias. Medical officials at Taiz’s main hospital warn stocks of lifesaving supplies will run out in less than two weeks.
Ilan Abdul-Khaliq: “We have more than 650 patients with kidney failure who risk losing their lives, as well as infants in incubators and patients in intensive care. … These disasters we’re facing and this situation necessitate international and humanitarian intervention to find safe passages for medicines, fuel, goods and food to enter the besieged city. Taiz is one of the most densely populated cities in Yemen, especially its city center.”
Earlier today, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen claimed its forces intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina area. The Houthis have denied carrying out any attacks on Saudi Arabia today. The conflicting claims came after Saudi officials said one person was wounded by falling debris Wednesday by an intercepted Houthi ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh. A Houthi spokesperson said the group had successfully struck King Khalid International Airport, following deadly attacks there over the weekend.
Two Cargo Ships Sunk Near Strait of Hormuz as Iran Steps Up Attacks
Oct 15, 2026
Two cargo ships sank near the Strait of Hormuz Wednesday after they were struck by unknown projectiles. The Cape Dao had been badly damaged in a September attack that killed a sailor. The GFS Pride sank a day after it suffered an explosion off the coast of Oman. Crew members were safely evacuated as the massive vessel sank, littering the ocean with some of its 2,500 cargo containers. This comes amid a recent surge of attacks on civilian ships by Iran’s military in response to the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and economic sanctions.
Meanwhile, the United Nations is urging the U.S. and Iran to agree to a plan to move fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz to prevent a global food crisis. About one-third of the world’s fertilizer shipments normally pass through the waterway. On Wednesday, a top U.N. official warned that unless a deal is put in place ahead of the planting season, commodity prices of food staples will soar, triggering a massive food security crisis affecting parts of Asia and Africa.
Ukraine Resumes Strikes on Russian Energy Sites as Zelensky Says He Feels “Betrayed” by Trump
Oct 15, 2026
In Ukraine, at least nine civilians were killed overnight and hundreds of thousands left without power after swarms of Russian drones attacked the capital Kyiv and Ukraine’s second-largest city Kharkiv. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it targeted plants supplying power and heating, as well as a data center in Kyiv. The attacks came days after President Trump unilaterally announced Russia and Ukraine had declared an “energy ceasefire” — an announcement both sides denied. This is a Kyiv resident who survived a Russian attack on her apartment complex Wednesday.
Olesya Gachechyladze: “I want to say to America and the whole world: Please help us. You said you would help us, but you’ve left us alone to face a great tragedy.”
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX’s satellite internet provider Starlink had cut bandwidth to objects traveling faster than 100 miles per hour, severely limiting drones, airplanes and helicopters used by Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in response that any limits to Starlink service in Ukraine are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, President Trump. That prompted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to say in an interview that he felt “betrayed” by Trump, who he said was on the wrong side of history. Zelensky also said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy sites. Ukrainian drones later struck an oil refinery south of Moscow, while another attack targeted a data center in Balakovo belonging to Russia’s largest state-controlled bank.
Seven Sailors Are Missing Off Romania’s Coast After Suspected Drone Attack in Black Sea
Oct 15, 2026
Romanian officials say seven sailors are missing after a fire broke out on a chemical tanker in Romanian territorial waters. This follows drone attacks on at least five other cargo ships in the Black Sea that some Romanian and Bulgarian officials have linked to Russia.
Trial of Ukrainian Ex-Officer Accused of Blowing Up Nord Stream Pipelines Gets Underway in Germany
Oct 15, 2026
In Germany, a trial got underway Wednesday for a Ukrainian military officer accused of leading a secret state-sponsored operation to blow up the Nord Stream pipelines, which were designed to deliver natural gas from Russia to Europe. The suspect, identified only as Serhii K., was a captain in a Ukrainian special forces unit at the time of the bombing in September 2022.
U.S. Deploys Hundreds of Soldiers to Assist “War on Drugs” in Colombia and Honduras
Oct 15, 2026
The U.S. is sending hundreds of soldiers to Latin America to train local forces to supposedly tackle drug trafficking. Soldiers from a 600-member battalion reportedly began deploying to a new jungle training facility in Panama. The troops are set to train with local forces in Colombia and Honduras. The Pentagon recently moved several MQ-9 Reaper drones from Africa to Colombia — and to Ecuador, where the U.S. military personnel and special forces are already operating.
The commander of U.S. Southern Command, General Francis Donovan, has said the U.S. plans to expand operations from strikes on boats to strikes on land. The U.S. has killed at least 239 people in boat strikes that legal experts have denounced as extrajudicial killings.
Costa Rica Opens High-Security Prison Modeled on El Salvador’s Notorious CECOT
Oct 15, 2026
Costa Rica has opened a new high-security prison designed to hold more than 5,000 prisoners. It’s modeled after the notorious CECOT mega-prison in El Salvador, where prisoners are denied due process and face torture, violence, medical neglect and other serious human rights abuses. On Wednesday, Costa Rica’s right-wing populist President Laura Fernández inaugurated the High-Containment Center Against Organized Crime, or CACCO, near the capital San José.
President Laura Fernández: “An investment of more than $35 million, precisely to contain the most dangerous convicts and cut off, once and for all, the power they have held within the prisons for decades. … We are going to use a firm hand, yes, because those who commit crimes must pay the price.”
President Fernández campaigned as a tough-on-crime candidate favoring harsher criminal sentencing and mandatory prison labor for convicts. She’s a close ally of El Salvador’s far-right President Nayib Bukele and President Donald Trump.
Publisher Pulls Sally Rooney’s Books from U.K. Shelves over Her Support of Palestine Action
Oct 15, 2026
The Irish author Sally Rooney says she has been forced to stop selling her books in the U.K. because of her support for Palestine Action, which the British government designates as a terrorist organization. In a statement to The Guardian, Rooney says that ever since she declared her support for the direct action group, she could no longer receive royalties from U.K. sales. She wrote, “The fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the U.K. could now constitute a serious criminal offense. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the U.K.” More than 3,700 people have been arrested in the U.K. for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since the group was banned last year.
Judge Pauses U.S. Sanctions on Pro-Palestinian Groups That Support International Criminal Court
Oct 15, 2026
Here in the United States, a federal judge in New York has granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Trump administration from enforcing sanctions against two U.S.-based groups that support the International Criminal Court’s work: the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide and DAWN, Democracy for the Arab World Now. The Trump administration sought to sanction the groups after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to former ICC Judge Navi Pillay, who chairs the U.N.’s Independent Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
NYC to Stop Investing Pension Funds in Israeli Bonds
Oct 15, 2026
The New York City comptroller, Democrat Mark Levine, says the city will not be investing its pension funds in Israeli bonds, since the quality of the bonds have deteriorated amid the wars in Gaza and Iran. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani welcomed the decision.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani: “I welcome the comptroller’s decision. It is something that I’ve said in the past, that I don’t believe that our city should purchase Israel bonds. We don’t purchase the bonds of any other sovereign nation. I don’t think that we should make an exception when it comes to Israel.”
U.S. Inflation Rate Hits 3.7%, Driven by Energy Prices
Oct 15, 2026
U.S. inflation ticked up to 3.7% in September, up from August’s gain of 3.4%. Prices rose faster than wages, which have increased 3% from a year ago. Economists attribute the rise in inflation to higher energy prices, as critics say the U.S. war on Iran and President Trump’s tariffs are contributing to increased costs.
Trump Continues Tour of Deep Red GOP Strongholds Ahead of Midterm Elections
Oct 15, 2026
President Trump is continuing his tour of traditional Republican strongholds ahead of November’s midterm elections, with plans to rally MAGA supporters in northern Kentucky on Saturday. On Wednesday, Trump traveled to Montana to support Republican congressional candidate Aaron Flint, who’s polling even with Democrat Sam Forstag. Earlier Wednesday, Trump traveled to a campaign event in Arizona aboard the new Air Force One, a luxury 747 jet given to him by the Qatari royal family.
President Donald Trump: “When they give you a 747, you say two words: ‘thank you.’”
Trump plans to take that jet with him when he leaves the White House.
Meanwhile, the mayor of Youngstown, Ohio, has condemned political violence at a campaign rally headlined by President Trump on Monday. Footage shows Trump mocking a protester wearing a shirt reading “Release the Epstein Files” as she is repeatedly punched by at least two members of the audience, to cheers and chants of “U.S.A.!” Uniformed officers then removed the protester from the venue. No charges have been filed.
WSJ: Trump Administration’s Probe of Rep. Ilhan Omar Aimed at Stripping Her Citizenship
Oct 15, 2026
The Trump administration’s investigation of Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar is aimed at building a case to strip away her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her, according to officials who spoke with The Wall Street Journal. The effort is focused at least in part on how Omar obtained her citizenship after she was brought to the U.S. as a child in 1995 following the outbreak of civil war in Somalia. Congressmember Omar’s office said in response, “President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this.” Among items seized by Homeland Security agents from Omar’s Washington, D.C., home on Monday were a cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and her passport.
Houston DA Considering Criminal Charges for ICE Agent Who Ran Over Fleeing Man
Oct 15, 2026
In Houston, Texas, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said his office will investigate an immigration agent running his vehicle over 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernández during an enforcement operation over the weekend. An ICE spokesperson said agents were trying to stop a vehicle carrying José Mendoza Cervantes, the person the operation was targeting, as well as Parra Hernández. But a lawyer for Parra Hernández said her client doesn’t know Mendoza Cervantes and that he was not with him on Saturday. In the footage, the ICE vehicle can be seen running over Parra Hernández. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare spoke with FOX 26 Houston.
Sean Teare: “He struck and ran over with a vehicle someone who didn’t even have an alien number yet, who had no history with ICE, who ICE wasn’t even looking for, much like Lorenzo Salgado, who was driving to work, who had never gotten as much as a speeding ticket in over 20 years here, and they shot and killed him. This is continuous behavior that is only designed to put fear in a large percentage of our population.”
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Failed California Bar Exam
Oct 15, 2026
The Wall Street Journal reports the new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia never passed the bar exam — despite President Trump referring to her as an attorney. Zacharia reportedly sat for the California Bar Exam in 2011 but failed it. The Campaign for Accountability has formally asked the California Bar to investigate whether Zacharia broke state law by falsely identifying herself as a lawyer.
Meanwhile, during a campaign rally in Arizona, President Trump suggested that those who leak information to the media should be shot.
President Donald Trump: “In my opinion, leakers should be shot. They should be shot. In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

By The Associated Press
Iran said Wednesday that a cargo ship has sunk after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, a top Iranian official said Iran must be prepared for war even as it is negotiating with the U.S. And a hospital in Gaza said a woman was killed in an Israeli strike.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran says a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine
A cargo ship sank after striking a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said. It was the first time Iran had reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war.
Shipping officials, meanwhile, said two Singapore-registered cargo vessels had been hit by “unknown projectiles” as they went through the strait on Tuesday and Wednesday. One sank, while the other reached safety. All crew members were evacuated from the first ship, and no injuries were reported in either incident, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.
“Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law,” the authority said.
It was unclear, however, if the Singapore-flagged vessel that sank was the same ship Iran said had struck a mine.
There were few details from Iranian officials, including about the fate of the crew. State television quoted a Guard statement saying the ship was traveling on what it called an illegal and dangerous route when it hit the mine Wednesday morning. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the images.
The unidentified ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The U.S. military has been guiding ships through the strait on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
Houthi rebel strike hits Saudi oil company’s headquarters
The headquarters of the Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco were hit in an overnight Houthi strike, two regional officials said, damaging the offices of the firm’s chief executive and other top officials. It was the latest demonstration of the Iran-backed rebels’ ability to attack high-profile targets.
There were no casualties in the attack, which the officials said targeted the top three floors of a building used by top executives in the city of Dhahran. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to discuss the matter with the media.
Earlier Wednesday, new explosions were heard in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, residents said, as blame again quickly fell on Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
The sight of smoke rising in recent days from some of Saudi Arabia’s most sensitive facilities has rattled the region and global oil markets while increasing questions for U.S. President Donald Trump, who has said he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
— By Samy Magdy in Cairo
Top Iran official says country must prepare for war as it negotiates
Iran must be prepared for war even as it negotiates with the U.S., the country’s parliament speaker said Wednesday.
Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said in a televised speech that his country’s main concern is preventing the United States from attacking again. But, he added, a signed agreement with Washington is no guarantee.
“They break their promises,” said Qalibaf. As a result, Iran must be prepared to fight “against a bullying enemy,” and “we must truly fight courageously on the battlefield.”
“That is when we will have achieved sustainable deterrence,” he said. “America must be punished. America must change its behavior. It must understand that it has to come to terms with the Iranian people.”
Israeli strike in Gaza City kills a woman
An Israeli strike on an apartment in Gaza City killed one woman early Wednesday, according to officials at Shifa hospital.
Israel’s military said it struck a Hamas fighter but was still assessing the strike’s outcome, without elaborating.
Just over a year since a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas went into effect, Israel still launches near-daily deadly strikes on the Palestinian enclave.
More than 1,490 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and combatants, but says almost half the dead are women and children.
This item has been corrected to show that almost half, not most, of the dead are women and children.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

body:
Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.
The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.
This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say.
They attribute Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to a ragtag group of Yemeni fighters to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, and the impact of the US war on Iran that has depleted stocks of interceptors.
TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN
Iran has been giving weapons, money and training to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo.
While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London.
"Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said.
"Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted."
Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran.
"The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles.
"Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told a press conference the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.
DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY
A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran.
The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment.
"China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said.
The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness.
Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle.
WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS
While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular.
"Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute.
Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said.
WAR EXPERIENCE
The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said.
A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea.
The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities.
"They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated."
Published on October 15, 2026
